papers.title: Deoxycholic Acid (DCA) a Secondary Bile Acid, Mitigates Ovariectomy-Induced Bone Loss and promotes Bone Healing: A Novel Candidate for Orthopaedic Applications
papers.abstract: Introduction Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMO) is a metabolic disorder, characterized by accelerated bone loss, gut microbiota (GM) dysbiosis and altered microbial metabolites. Deoxycholic acid (DCA) is a secondary bile acid with an FDA-approved drug status for submental fat treatment in adults; however its effect on bone health remains underexplored. Materials and Methods This study investigated the effects of DCA on bone health using both preclinical animal model of PMO and clinical samples from PMO women. DCA (20 mg/kg) was administered to ovariectomised (OVX) mice for 45 days, and its effects on bone microarchitecture and serum cytokines were analysed. Osteoclastogenesis and osteoblastogenesis were evaluated using murine and human samples. Untargeted and targeted metabolomics analyses were performed using an ultra-high-performance liquid chromatographic system coupled with high-resolution Orbitrap mass spectrometry (HRMS). Secondary analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data was performed using R programming. Results GM analysis and plasma metabolomics revealed an alteration in bacterial taxa associated with secondary BA synthesis and reduced circulating DCA levels. DCA administration improved impaired trabecular and cortical bone microarchitecture in the OVX mice by inhibiting osteoclastogenesis and enhancing osteoblastogenesis. Moreover, DCA altered circulating osteoclastogenic (IL-6, Il-9, IL-17A, IFN-{gamma}, RANKL) and osteoblastogenic (OPG, TGF-{beta}, IL-10) factors. Mechanically, DCA suppressed osteoclast differentiation and the expression of genes associated with osteoclast formation (NFATC1, NFKB, TRAF6, TREM2, SYNB), fusion (CSF1R, DC-STAMP, CD47), and resorption (CTSK, ATP6VOD1, ATP6VOD2, CAR2, SPP1) in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), while promoting osteogenic differentiation and matrix mineralization in bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) from PMO women. Additionally, DCA enhanced the nascent calcium deposition at the fracture site and improved bone healing via inhibiting osteoclastogenesis. Conclusion Overall, reduced DCA availability was associated with PMO, while DCA treatment mitigated OVX-induced bone loss and improved bone healing. This study highlights the therapeutic potential of DCA for maintaining both bone homeostasis in PMO and fracture healing with immense orthopaedic applications.

papers.title: A metastable GαS/β-arrestin complex sustains endosomal PTH1R signaling
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) initiate cellular signaling by activating heterotrimeric G proteins at the plasma membrane and are silenced when beta-arrestin binds the phosphorylated receptor, preventing G protein binding. However, many receptors continue to generate cAMP after internalization, even while barr is bound, a paradox that lacked a molecular mechanism in live cells. A direct barrestin1-Gas interface in the PTH1R-barr1-Gas complex has recently been defined structurally, but whether the complex operates in endosomes, and how it behaves there, has not been established. Using intact cells, we examine the assembly at three spatial resolutions. Confocal imaging with a nanobody selective for nucleotide-free Gas places activated Gas, barr, and agonist-occupied PTH1R on the same endosomes. Single-molecule localization microscopy, with illumination modes that separate the plasma membrane from the endosomal membrane in single cells, shows that the agonist recruits Gas and barr at both membranes. FRET, however, reveals a specific interaction only on endosomes, where a Gas inhibitor restricted to that compartment abolishes the sustained cAMP phase without affecting receptor internalization. Weighted-ensemble-enhanced molecular simulations show that the complex is metastable, releasing Gas through a large rigid-body rotation away from barr while barr itself tightens its interactions with the receptor. These findings provide a molecular basis for endosomal Gs/cAMP signaling and open a new avenue for drug development targeting this pathway.

papers.title: Advancing AOPs for genotoxicity through quantifying KERs linking DNA alkylation to increase in mutations and chromosome aberrations
papers.abstract: Quantitative Adverse Outcome Pathways (qAOPs) help translate mechanistic knowledge into quantitative toxicity predictions; however, their development is constrained by the limited availability and heterogeneity of quantitative data. Here, we investigated the feasibility of developing a qAOP for genotoxicity by modeling quantitative relationships linking DNA alkylation to increased mutations and structural chromosome aberrations through intermediate biological key events (KEs). We compiled and harmonized published concentration-response data from human lymphoblastoid TK6 cells exposed to ethyl methanesulfonate, methyl methanesulfonate, or N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea, covering eight genotoxicity assays representing five KEs with well-established dependencies. We evaluated sources of variability, compared points of departure (PoDs), and quantified relationships between successive events using response-response modeling. Substantial between-study variability could to a limited extent be explained through differences in experimental design while batch effects for individual studies and researchers were substantial. PoD estimates that were calculated from combined results of independent studies with similar experimental design, were often uncertain due to insufficient concentration-response characterization or conflicting results between studies. Nevertheless, response-response modeling suggested a threshold effect for certain key-event relationships (KERs). Specifically, DNA adducts seemed to be triggered at lower concentrations of alkylating agents compared to the subsequent KEs of DNA strand breaks and chromosome aberrations. Furthermore, these fitted response-response models can be used for prediction of downstream KEs from earlier ones. The general approach we developed for BMC analysis followed by response-response modeling is applicable to other AOPs as well. These findings highlight both the feasibility and limitations of using existing data for qAOP development.

papers.title: Denaturation-sensitive BRET probes enable intracellular thermal shift measurements across diverse protein targets and biomolecular complexes
papers.abstract: Thermal shift assays have revolutionized drug discovery, but can be limited in sensitivity and scalability. Combining the unique attributes of differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) and cellular thermal shift (CETSA), we report the methodological framework for the bioluminescence resonance energy transfer shift assay (BRETSA). BRETSA utilizes denaturation sensitive BRET probes, in combination with luciferase-tagged target proteins, to track and longitudinally record thermal shift in living cells. Denaturation profiles were successfully measured for over 500 globular proteins, spanning 24 target families in diverse cellular compartments. Among these, target engagement was confirmed for over 200 proteins; including validated drug targets as well as understudied members of the kinase subfamily. Leveraging orthosteric, allosteric, and covalent ligands in potency studies, this method offers improved sensitivity and scalability compared to other thermal shift methods. We extend the utility of BRETSA to interrogate target engagement at biomolecular complexes and query cooperative binding for molecular glues and emerging tricomplex drug modalities.

papers.title: Social costs of group life: Larger groups have less affiliative behavior and more social conflict
papers.abstract: The costs and benefits of sociality depend in part upon the size of groups. Therefore, individual behavior should vary across groups of different sizes, reflecting group size-dependent costs and benefits. Here, we test this prediction using a long-term dataset on wild female baboons (Papio cynocephalus x P. anubis). We find that individuals who live in larger groups suffer social costs: compared to animals in smaller groups, they experience more agonistic interactions, fewer grooming interactions, and sparser social networks. These social costs arise, in part, from a pattern in which relationships within dyads become more agonistic as group size increases (i.e., a given dyad exhibits fewer grooming interactions relative to agonistic interactions when it is living in a larger group). While individuals in large groups generally maintain the same number of strong bonds as individuals in small groups, they tend to develop weak bonds with a greater number of social partners that results in, on average, weaker bonds overall. Our results demonstrate that, despite potential benefits to large groups in terms of predation risk and intergroup competition, the social lives of individuals in larger groups involve less affiliation and more conflict in this wild primate population.

papers.title: Deconstructing Boldness: Latent behavioural structure across novelty, predation, and exploration in an endangered species translocation program
papers.abstract: Risk-related behaviours including neophobia, exploration, and predator avoidance are often assumed to covary along a general boldness axis. Although some translocation studies have linked one or more of these behaviours with fitness, it is possible that the underlying behavioural structure varies under different selective environments. Conservation breeding programs provide a unique opportunity to evaluate the structure of behavioural correlations in a non-domestic species under artificial conditions. We tested whether risk-related behaviours represent a unified boldness syndrome in a captive population of the endangered Attwaters prairie chicken (APC; Tympanuchus cupido attwateri). We quantified the repeatable behaviours of 257 juveniles and compared 11 models of behavioural covariation structure using multivariate mixed models and confirmatory factor analysis. There was no support for a single risk-taking axis; instead, we found three dimensions representing responses to novelty and environmental stimuli (Engagement), predator avoidance (Threat Response), and maze exploration (Maze Progression). Our results indicate that these risk-related behaviours are not organized along a single axis in captive APCs, challenging assumptions that risk-taking represents a universal behavioural syndrome. To anticipate post-release success accurately, conservation managers should understand the exact behavioural architecture of the captive population rather than assume that the classical bold-shy structure occurs in all contexts.

papers.title: Peptide Sequence Determines the Efficacy of Single-Dose AAV-Vectorized GLP-1R Agonists in Diet-Induced Obese Mice
papers.abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists such as semaglutide produce substantial weight loss and glycemic improvement, but their long-term efficacy depends on sustained adherence to chronic dosing. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy could, in principle, provide durable GLP-1R agonist (GLP-1RA) exposure from a single administration, but the degree of peptide engineering required for a vectorized GLP-1RA transgene to be efficacious in vivo is unknown. Methods: We generated four self-complementary AAV (scAAV) constructs encoding: native human GLP-1(7-36) (GLP-1), a DPP-IV-resistant Gly8-GLP-1(7-36) variant (Gly8), Exendin-4 (Ex4), or an Exendin-4 human IgG4 Fc fusion protein (Ex4-Fc). All four constructs were validated to secrete functional GLP-1R agonists in vitro using a conditioned-media potency assay. Subsequently, these constructs were packaged into PHP.eB capsids and administered as a single intravenous dose (5x1012 vg/kg) to diet-induced obese (DIO) mice alongside a vehicle control. Body weight, body composition, food intake, fasting plasma insulin, and oral glucose tolerance were assessed over a 3-week period. At the end of the study, tissues were harvested for assessments of plasma/liver lipids, tissue transgene transcript and peptide levels. Results: HEK293 cells transfected with the four AAV constructs all secreted active peptides/proteins as assessed by a cell-based GLP-1R activation assay, although the effective concentration of the GLP-1 constructs in the media spanned nearly four orders of magnitude 72 hours after transfection. In diet-induced obese (DIO) mice, Ex4 and Ex4-Fc vectors, but not GLP-1 or Gly8 vectors, produced significant reductions in body weight of up to 22.6% of starting body weight out to 21 days after a single dose. In addition, reductions in food intake, fat mass, and fasting insulin relative to vehicle were also observed for Ex4 and Ex4-Fc. Furthermore, Ex4-Fc improved oral glucose tolerance while reducing plasma cholesterol and liver triglycerides relative to vehicle. Although transcript levels did not differ appreciably among the four constructs in either brain or liver, measurable peptide product in plasma and brain lysate tracked the rank order of the in vitro supernatant screen, with GLP-1 and Gly8 groups indistinguishable from endogenous background. Conclusions: PHP.eB scAAV Ex4 and Ex4-Fc showed robust efficacy on multiple metabolic endpoints including weight loss and glucose tolerance. In contrast, vectorized GLP-1 and Gly8 showed no in vivo efficacy despite comparable levels of viral transcript in the brain and the liver. Vectorized GLP-1 and Gly8 also performed poorly compared to exendin-4-based constructs in vitro, suggesting that conditioned-media potency screening is a valid early filter for construct selection in vectorized-peptide AAV development. Engineering peptides to improve translation and secretion efficiency, in addition to circulating plasma stability, could further optimize vectorized GLP-1RA therapeutics.

papers.title: Molecular Mechanisms of Quizartinib Resistance in FLT3 Mutants
papers.abstract: Quizartinib, a type II FLT3 inhibitor approved for FLT3-ITD-positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML), is frequently limited by acquired resistance, which arises in up to 40% of patients with disease progression and is driven largely by the D835Y and F691L kinase-domain mutations. To define the underlying mechanisms, we performed triplicate 200-ns all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type FLT3, FLT3-D835Y, and FLT3-F691L in complex with Quizartinib, combining conformational analysis, MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations, and binding-pocket characterization. Both mutations destabilized the inactive DFG-out conformation required for type II inhibitor binding, with mean binding free-energy reductions of 5 kcal/mol for D835Y and 10 kcal/mol for F691L relative to wild-type. D835Y disrupted the activation-loop electrostatic network and reduced Cys694 hydrogen-bond occupancy from 85% to 45%, whereas F691L abolished key van der Waals contacts and opened a 120 cubic Angstrom hydrophobic void at the gatekeeper position. Both mutants sampled a wider range of conformations and lost 14-17% of binding-pocket volume. These predictions were corroborated by CCK-8 viability assays and Western blotting of p-FLT3 (Y591) in Ba/F3 cells, which reproduced the predicted resistance hierarchy (F691L > D835Y > WT) at the cellular level. Together, these results indicate that D835Y and F691L confer resistance through distinct electrostatic and hydrophobic mechanisms that converge on destabilization of the inactive kinase conformation, providing a structural basis for the design of next-generation FLT3 inhibitors.

papers.title: Preclinical Evaluation of a Novel BOC-Modified Triazoloacridinone (TRA-01AR) in Combination with 5-Fluorouracil in Colorectal Cancer
papers.abstract: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) remains a cornerstone of colorectal cancer (CRC) therapy, yet its clinical efficacy is limited by resistance, systemic toxicity, and unfavorable pharmacokinetics. Strategies that enhance tumor sensitivity while maintaining tolerability are therefore of considerable interest. Here, we evaluated 5-FU in combination with two triazoloacridinones, C-1305 and a novel BOC-modified derivative, TRA-01AR, using integrated cellular, transcriptomic, bioenergetic, and in vivo approaches. Both compounds induced cytotoxic effects across cancer cell models and produced overlapping but distinct transcriptional responses, primarily affecting DNA replication and cell cycle pathways. Bioenergetic profiling revealed a shift toward oxidative phosphorylation accompanied by reduced glycolysis, indicating modulation of cellular metabolism relevant to chemotherapy response. Interestingly, TRA-01AR exhibited delayed cytotoxicity relative to C-1305, although the underlying mechanism remains to be defined. In vivo, the combination of 5-FU with C-1305 significantly reduced tumor weight in HT-29 xenografts, whereas 5-FU combined with TRA-01AR did not result in a statistically significant reduction compared to 5-FU alone. TRA-01AR was associated with a more favorable systemic profile and increased intratumoral blood flow compared with C-1305. Collectively, these findings indicate that triazoloacridinones modulate transcriptional and metabolic programs relevant to the 5-FU response. While C-1305 demonstrated greater antitumor activity under the tested conditions, TRA-01AR exhibited distinct biological effects, including improved tolerability and vascular modulation. Further studies are required to clarify TRA-01AR's mechanism of action and assess its potential relevance in CRC-specific therapies.

papers.title: Inductive bias anchors a scaling law for biological learning
papers.abstract: The speed of animal learning varies substantially across individuals and task domains, and does not always track intuitive notions of task complexity. A nominally simple binary decision task can take thousands of rewards to reach proficiency, whereas seemingly complex naturalistic tasks can be learned within dozens. A long-standing explanation is that learning speed reflects the alignment between an animal's inductive biases and the task at hand. However, without a precise notion of alignment, it is difficult to translate this idea into quantitative predictions. Here, modeling an animal as a Bayesian learner that improves through iterative reward feedback, we use statistical learning theory to derive a scaling law for biological learning. The law makes two predictions. First, inductive bias multiplicatively sets the speed of learning through a single quantity, the effective complexity. This quantity measures how well the task aligns with the animal's prior, and corresponds to the number of bits required to represent the task solution under that prior. We demonstrate this multiplicative scaling in a human motor learning dataset, where behavioral measurements before learning can precisely predict subsequent learning speed. Second, task performance improves as a power law in experience. We validate this power law in a large-scale mouse learning dataset and show that a two-parameter rescaling collapses individual learning curves onto a universal function predicted by the theory. These results suggest that behavioral measurements before learning can be used to predict task-dependent learning speeds, and they explain why learning speed reflects alignment with prior knowledge rather than nominal task complexity.

papers.title: The Where and When of Tracking Sound Sources Head-based auditory motion tracking integrates velocity and spatial error within a common delayed frame
papers.abstract: Auditory objects in everyday environments remain seldomly at the same position but move about in the environment and keeping track of their motion is an essential task for the auditory system to maintain a correct representation of auditory space/scene. Following such a moving sound source in two-dimensional space requires the nervous system to guide head movements using delayed and uncertain sensory information. How the auditory system integrates such information for combined horizontal and vertical movements is still debated. 116 117 We recorded head movements from 14 participants tracking a physically moving loudspeaker along unpredictable two-dimensional trajectories. Participants followed source motion with substantial delays and retained measurable spatial discrepancies. To explain these behaviours, we developed a hybrid model combining source velocity with the spatial discrepancy between source and head at the matched, delayed time points. The model predicts head velocity on previously unseen trajectories more accurately than formulations relying on either signal alone. Importantly, using preceding rather than current head orientation improved prediction, highlighting the importance of temporal correspondence between sensory and motor states. These findings suggest that head-based auditory motion tracking depends on complementary motion and spatial information represented within a common delayed reference frame.

papers.title: Shared brain transcriptome signatures of social evolution and plasticity in shell-dwelling cichlid fishes
papers.abstract: Inter-individual variability in phenotypic traits is widespread in nature both across and within species, with similar patterns of variation often occurring between and within species. Given that these two types of variation are generated by evolutionary and plasticity processes respectively, it raises the question to what extent the causal mechanisms underlying such variability at these two different levels are shared or not. To address this question, we studied the variation in brain transcriptomes in Tanganyikan cichlids that exhibit both intra- and interspecific variation in social behavior. We compared two facultatively social cichlid species, each containing naturally occurring solitary and social-living individuals, with a closely related obligatory solitary resembling the ancestral state. Differential gene expression and Gene Set Enrichment Analyses were performed in the telencephalon and diencephalon transcriptomes to investigate the molecular basis of both behavioral plasticity and the evolution of sociality. Behavioral plasticity involved few differentially expressed genes but extensive changes in biological pathways, supporting a highly polygenic architecture of social behavior. Across both species, social-living individuals consistently upregulated pathways involved in translation, protein homeostasis, and energy metabolism, whereas solitary individuals showed enrichment of neuronal morphogenesis, cell adhesion, and structural plasticity. Remarkably, these same functional programs were associated with the independent evolution of sociality, revealing a strong overlap between evolutionary and plastic transcriptional responses. This convergence was largely restricted to the telencephalon, while the diencephalon showed limited and inconsistent functional signatures. Together, our results support the repeated recruitment of gene regulatory programs during the evolution of sociality and demonstrate that behavioral plasticity and evolutionary transitions share common neurogenomic responses, consistent with a conserved genetic toolkit for social behavior.

papers.title: The role of familiarity in grouping decisions of Trinidadian guppies
papers.abstract: Social grouping is widely observed in numerous taxa, providing individuals with a variety of benefits including efficient information exchange and predator protection. However, grouping can also carry costs such as increased competition for resources, which means that individuals must often make decisions regarding joining or leaving a group. These decisions to leave or stay might in turn depend on prior experience with potential groupmates. Past work has shown that many fish distinguish between familiar and unfamiliar conspecifics and use these distinctions in their grouping choices. Trinidadian guppies (Poecilia reticulata), well known for their diversity in shoaling preferences, are an excellent system in which to investigate the role of familiarity in grouping decisions. We examined preferences for familiar individuals following both a 15-day and 55-day cohabitation period in two different guppy populations. Utilizing two binary-choice designs, we found no evidence for a familiarity preference in either population, despite observing a high preference to group with conspecifics in both populations. These results suggest that various contextual- and population-level differences may impact familiarity preferences, in turn contributing to the growing body of work on the evolution of social organization and grouping decisions in teleost species and beyond.

papers.title: Divergence in sleep architecture associated with interspecific shifts in memory investment
papers.abstract: Sleep plays a critical role in stabilising memory. However, whether the architecture of sleep co-evolves with investment in learning and memory is unknown. To address this, we exploit the extreme levels of neural and behavioural divergence among Heliconiini butterflies. Compared to other Heliconiini, Heliconius have massively expanded mushroom bodies, the insect centres of learning and memory, which are associated with specific enhancements in visual learning and memory. Using a purpose-built video system, machine learning-facilitated behavioural tracking, and in-depth analysis of micro-behaviours during nighttime quiescence, we describe multi-state sleep in Heliconius melpomene and an outgroup Heliconiini, Dryas iulia. In both species, sleep is predominantly composed of quiet sleep, however, Heliconius and Dryas deviate in specific features. In Dryas iulia, quiet sleep is characterised by highly stereotyped, rhythmic antennal oscillations. Conversely, the antennae of Heliconius melpomene remain largely motionless but occasionally perform large movements which interrupt quiet sleep. These antennal deflections are associated with bouts of activity that include increased overall antennal displacement, isolated head twitching, proboscis movements and less frequently, wing movements. While these episodes were also seen in Dryas iulia, they were considerably less frequent. We further demonstrate that the behavioural profile of these active sleep bouts is constituently different from bouts of induced wakefulness, providing experimental support for multi-state sleep in Lepidoptera. This work shows that Heliconius melpomene, a species distinguished by its expanded mushroom bodies, exhibits more frequent bouts of active sleep than the outgroup species Dryas iulia. These findings raise the possibility that increased investment in learning and memory, as well as the structures that support it, may be associated with changes in sleep architecture.

papers.title: Neonatal personality is associated with sex-specific developmental trajectories in a wild mammal
papers.abstract: Animal personality, defined as consistent among-individual differences in behaviour, is an important source of phenotypic variation, but its developmental origins and associations with subsequent development remain poorly understood. We measured neonatal personalities, early-life growth, and yearling male antler length in wild fallow deer (Dama dama). Using eight years of data, we estimated repeatability and among-individual correlations among neonatal personalities and growth and applied structural equation modelling to examine associations with yearling male morphology. Heart rate and behavioural reaction measures showed repeatable among-individual variation, demonstrating that stable differences were detectable shortly after birth. Behavioural reaction was negatively correlated with growth in males but not in females. Heart rate was not associated with growth in either sex. In males, the effects of neonatal behavioural reactivity persisted beyond early life: more behaviourally reactive neonates had shorter antlers as yearlings, indirectly through reduced early-life growth. These findings show that stable among-individual differences emerge during the neonatal period and are associated with sex-specific developmental trajectories.

papers.title: Causal Multiscale Modeling of Ocular FLASH Electroretinography: Model Development, Experimental Fitting, and Spin-Glass--Percolation Predictions
papers.abstract: textbf{Purpose:} To develop a causal multiscale model of retinal electroretinography (ERG) after ocular ultrahigh-dose-rate (FLASH) and conventional-dose-rate (CONV) irradiation, evaluate the framework against published ocular ERG data, and derive prospective dose-response predictions for future validation. textbf{Methods:} The retina was coarse-grained into $N=200$ functional modules. Local rate equations were formulated as Hodgkin--Huxley-inspired conductance-balance/RC reductions of retinal ion-channel and synaptic pathways. Radiation generated an injury field that altered phototransduction, a-wave and b-wave dynamics and, in the network extension, inter-module coupling and bond survival. A reduced amplitude benchmark and nested M0/M1/M2 causal models were evaluated. textbf{Results:} The reduced benchmark achieved $R^2=0.9721$ and RMSE $=11.94~mu$V. M0, M1, and M2 yielded $R^2=0.8546$, 0.8559, and 0.8560, respectively, indicating limited independent identifiability of the network terms from amplitude data alone. Under an exploratory 50% retained-gain criterion, the reduced benchmark predicted a-wave preservation thresholds of 28.6 Gy for FLASH and 23.7 Gy for CONV, and b-wave thresholds of 29.2 Gy and 24.1 Gy, respectively, corresponding to a model-based functional dose-modifying factor (DMF) of 1.21. textbf{Conclusion:} The ERG amplitude data support the causal radiation-injury-to-ERG framework, while additional observables will be needed to distinguish the predicted collective-network contributions. The model also provides quantitative dose targets for prospective studies of the FLASH retinal-preservation window and a framework for testing how local retinal injury may propagate into collective dysfunction.

papers.title: Cisplatin-triggered sensory dysfunction in NER-defective C. elegans involves GABAergic and cholinergic signaling
papers.abstract: Cisplatin (CisPt) is a widely used anticancer drug that causes neurotoxicity as a dose-limiting adverse effect. DNA damage contributes to CisPt-induced neurotoxicity, yet the molecular mechanisms involved remain unclear. Here, we aim to identify pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to DNA damage-driven development of sensory neuronal dysfunction using the 3R-compliant model organism Caenorhabditis elegans. To this end, we employed the nucleotide excision repair (NER)-deficient ercc-1 mutant, which shows enhanced CisPt-induced sensory dysfunction as monitored by the chemotaxis assay, to elucidate drug-induced alterations in neurotransmission and transcriptome. We found that CisPt reduces gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels in the nematode and that GABA supplementation rescues ercc-1 mutants from CisPt-evoked sensory neurotoxicity, pointing to a neuroprotective function of GABA in the context of our study. Moreover, CisPt impairs the morphological integrity of GABAergic neurons particularly in ercc-1 mutants, which again is rescued by GABA substitution. Conversely, the cholinergic agonist carbachol impairs sensory function and exacerbates the neurotoxic effects of CisPt in ercc-1 mutants, indicating detrimental effects resulting from cholinergic excitation. Transcriptome analysis revealed that CisPt treatment stimulates a broard transcriptional response, including pathways involved in the regulation of neuronal communication, including acetylcholine-mediated neurotransmission, with pronounced effects occurring in the absence of ERCC-1. Based on these finding we suggest impaired GABAergic signaling and the loss of neuronal integrity GABAergic neurons as well as excessive cholinergic excitation as key mechanisms linking CisPt-induced DNA damage in NER defective nematodes to sensory dysfunction. Hence, targeting the balance between GABAergic inhibition and cholinergic excitation is suggested to counteract sensory neurotoxicity triggered by CisPt.

papers.title: PCB-Exposed Gut Microbiota Recapitulate Neurobehavioral Deficits and Reprogram Hippocampal Transcriptomic Signatures
papers.abstract: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are persistent environmental pollutants associated with developmental neurotoxicity and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, whether PCB-induced alterations in gut microbiota contribute to neurodevelopmental toxicity independently of direct chemical exposure remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether transplantation of PCB-associated gut microbiota produces early neurobehavioral alterations and disrupts brain molecular pathways in offspring. Gut microbiota from conventional dams exposed to the Fox River PCB mixture (FRM; 6.0 mg/kg/day) or vehicle were transplanted into germ-free recipient females without direct PCB administration. At postnatal day 7 (P7), offspring underwent ultrasonic vocalization (USV) testing, whole-brain RNA sequencing (n = 4/sex/group), and untargeted serum metabolomics. Untargeted serum metabolomics were also performed in donor dams. PCB-associated fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) significantly reduced offspring USVs, reproducing effects observed following direct maternal PCB exposure. Brain transcriptomics in offspring identified substantially more differentially expressed genes in males (9,339) than females (1,082), including 512 shared genes. Concordantly regulated genes revealed downregulation of neurotransmitter signaling and ion channel pathways alongside upregulation of RNA processing pathways. Male-associated responses involved altered protein synthesis and neuronal signaling, whereas female-associated responses involved DNA repair and extracellular matrix remodeling. Despite these molecular differences, behavioral responses showed no significant sex-dependent effect. Maternal metabolomics revealed increased bile acids and decreased indole-3-propionic acid, highlighting potential AhR-NF{kappa}B and bile acid-associated signaling mechanisms. Offspring metabolomics further identified alterations in lipid-associated metabolites and metabolic profiles. Collectively, these findings show that transferring PCB-exposed microbiota reproduces early neurobehavioral alterations and induces shared and sex-biased molecular responses, identifying the maternal gut microbiome as a candidate mediator linking PCB exposure to developmental neurotoxicity.

papers.title: Personality and dominance shape core area use and territory-related signalling in a feral ungulate
papers.abstract: Space use strategies determine how animals acquire resources and encounter competitors, which ultimately influence their survival. Instead of utilising their entire range uniformly, animals typically concentrate activity in locations where resources are most valuable, and these 'core areas' provide key insights into the behavioural strategies underlying space use. Although competitive ability is often expected to influence core area use, substantial individual-level variation remains unexplained. Consistent behavioural differences among individuals, or personality, may contribute to this variation, but their role in shaping spatial behaviour under natural conditions is poorly understood. To address this gap, we observed adult males (n=24) from a free-ranging, semi-urban population of Asian water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis). We quantified individual core area size and territory-related signalling behaviour, and assessed personality from >9,300 minutes of observations. Most males (79%) shared overlapping core areas with one to five other males but with clear dominance relationships. Social engagement, reflecting a social personality, was positively associated with core area size in subordinates, but not in dominant males. Social engagement was also positively associated with territory-related signalling frequency. By contrast, a non-social personality labelled as activity-maintenance did not influence with core area size or signalling behaviour. We also found that dominant males exhibited lower signalling frequencies than subordinates. Overall, we show that personality and dominance are associated with distinct aspects of spatial behaviour. These findings demonstrate that individual spatial strategies emerge from the interplay between behavioural phenotypes and social lives, highlighting the spatial-social interface as a source of variation in animal space use.

papers.title: Aging, HIV Status, and Sex Differentially Influence Antiretroviral Therapy Disposition Pathways in Rectosigmoid Tissue and Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
papers.abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are increasingly surviving into older age due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral (ARV) therapy (ART), creating a growing population in whom age-related changes may influence treatment outcomes. Although aging is known to affect drug disposition, the molecular mechanisms by which aging alters ARV pharmacology remain incompletely understood, particularly within tissue compartments, including the rectosigmoid region of the colon, that serve as sites of HIV transmission and persistence. To address this knowledge gap, we used proteomics by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to evaluate the impact of age and HIV status on proteins and pathways relevant to ARV disposition in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and rectosigmoid colon tissue obtained from young (18-50) HIV-seronegative adults, older (65-80) HIV-seronegative adults, and older virally suppressed people living with HIV. We found that aging and HIV infection differentially influenced proteins predominantly within nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pathways, in rectosigmoid tissue and PBMC. HIV-associated effects to the proteome were more prominent in PBMC, whereas aging produced broader alterations in ARV disposition-related proteins in rectosigmoid tissue, including proteins involved in drug transport, intracellular drug activation, dephosphorylation, and nucleotide homeostasis. Several age-associated changes were further influenced by biologic sex, suggesting that aging may not affect ARV disposition uniformly across populations. To place these findings within a broader context, pathway analyses were performed that identified extensive tissue-specific remodeling associated with aging and HIV infection involving drug disposition, immune regulation, cellular metabolism, and disease-related pathways. Notably, aging was associated with alterations in pathways relevant to nucleotide metabolism and gastrointestinal tissue function, suggesting that processes beyond traditional drug transport and metabolism pathways may contribute to variability in ARV disposition with advancing age. Together, these findings identify aging as an important modifier of pathways that regulate ARV disposition within compartments relevant to HIV transmission and persistence. While the clinical consequences of our findings are unknown, these data provide a mechanistic foundation for future studies investigating whether age-associated changes influence the effectiveness of ART and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in older adults.

papers.title: Hide and seek in a rainforest canopy : when a fruit-eating carnivore (almost) met its top predator carnivore
papers.abstract: Prey-predator interactions in the wild are spectacular. Common reported cases come from ground-dwelling animals, in open areas and by daylight. Here, we report, for the first time, a sequence with the nocturnal arboreal kinkajou (Potos flavus), being followed ca. 20 minutes apart by one of its predators, the puma (Puma concolor), 33 m aboveground in a rainforest in French Guiana.

papers.title: Sex differences in agonistic social behavior: Effects of exercise and ovariectomy
papers.abstract: Aggressive behavior encompasses a range of offensive and defensive responses that may be differentially influenced by sex, ovarian hormones, and physical activity. However, much of the existing research has focused on males and utilized paradigms designed to elicit aggression, leaving the expression and regulation of offensive and defensive behaviors during other forms of social interaction poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of sex, voluntary wheel running (VWR), and ovariectomy (OVX) on agonistic behavior during juvenile social exploration in adult Sprague-Dawley rats. Males exhibited greater offensive aggression, characterized by increased aggressive grooming and pinning, whereas females displayed more defensive kicking, darting, and avoidance. OVX selectively reduced defensive kicking without significantly affecting offensive aggression or avoidance, suggesting that distinct behavioral responses differ in their sensitivity to ovarian hormone removal. In contrast, VWR did not significantly alter any of the behaviors examined. Importantly, exploratory composite analyses revealed a significant sex difference in offensive aggression that was no longer detected when defensive behaviors were incorporated into the measure. Together, these findings demonstrate that sex differences in agonistic behavior extend beyond overall levels of aggression to distinct patterns of offensive and defensive responses. Distinguishing these behavioral categories may therefore be important for identifying how various manipulations, such as sex, ovarian hormones, and physical activity, influence agonistic behavior.

papers.title: Organism-dependent ecotoxicological effects of transition metal-containing layered double hydroxides
papers.abstract: Due to low environmental stability of certain molecule classes, such as phytohormones and RNA interference, layered double hydroxides (LDHs) have been investigated as nanocarriers capable of protecting and transporting molecules of interest in natural systems. Herein, the ecotoxicological effects of LDH nanoparticles composed by different transition metals (Al-Ni, Al-Co, and Al-Cu) were evaluated in maize (Zea mays), tomato (Lycopersicum esculentum), and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, two important crops and one soil organism found in agricultural systems. Plants were exposed to the nanoparticles through foliar spraying (5, 50, and 500 ug/mL), and physiological parameters were evaluated. In C. elegans, lethality, locomotion, larval development, and body length were analyzed. The nanoparticles exhibited high colloidal stability and characteristic lamellar morphology. The results demonstrated low phytotoxicity for all formulations, without significant changes in photochemical activity, effective quantum yield of photosystem II (psi-PSII), stomatal conductance (gs), and chlorophyll index (Chl a+b; ICF) in plants. In contrast, C. elegans exhibited greater sensitivity, showing reduced motility, developmental delay, and decreased body length, although mortality remained below 12% under all evaluated conditions. Toxicity was dependent on the metallic composition, following the order Al-Cu > Al-Ni > Al-Co. Collectively, the results indicate that LDHs exhibit high compatibility with those two crops but may cause sublethal effects in soil organisms. These findings highlight the importance of multispecies ecotoxicological assessments for the safe development of nanocarriers intended for agricultural applications.

papers.title: Can a Tiny Brain Plan? Reconstructing a Predatory Detour inthe Jumping Spider Portia labiata
papers.abstract: Planning is the process of evaluating alternative futures to predict outcomes and guide action. Evidence for this process exists in several vertebrates, but remains contested in in-vertebrates. Jumping spiders in the genus Portia show planning-like behavior in lab studies, but how this translates to the wild is unclear, where hunts of potentially lethal spider prey occur over durations of more than an hour in dense foliage. We present the first fully video-recorded wild hunt of any Portia species, with a 3D reconstruction of its forty-two minute long route to attack an orb-weaving spider. The reconstruction suggests P. labiata may have planned its approach, avoiding a route half as long but potentially more conspicuous to the prey's sensory systems.

papers.title: Moving Heads, Moving Sounds: Systematic Errors in Auditory Motion Perception
papers.abstract: The movement of moving objects seen during self-motion is incorrectly perceived as a result of errors in parsing the visual motion arising from the retina and from information about the movement of the head and eyes in space1. The perception of motion of auditory targets may be even more challenging as previous research suggests that the auditory system lacks dedicated low-level speed processing mechanisms. This study investigates how the perception of a moving auditory sound source is influenced by concurrent head movements, drawing comparisons with established visual motion perception findings and illusions, such as the Filehne Illusion. Participants were asked to move their heads at a fixed speed, either horizontally (left to right or right to left) or vertically (up to down or down to up), while indicating the perceived direction of a moving sound source by using a joystick. A physical sound source was moved silently at a constant speed in fronto-parallel 2D space using a 3x3x3m cable robot. Results showed that head movements created a perceptual bias of the perceived direction of the moving sound source in the opposite direction to the head movement. Responses were less precise during horizontal than vertical head movement, whereas overall directional accuracy did not differ reliably between movement planes. The magnitude of the directional error also depended on the direction of head movement, consistent with the different cues available for horizontal and vertical localization (binaural vs. spectral cues). These findings suggest that similarly to how visual motion perception is distorted by extraretinal signals and the movement of the eyes, so too is auditory motion perception influenced by movement of the ears, revealing errors in the integration of proprioceptive, vestibular and auditory cues that distort the perceived direction of a moving sound source.

papers.title: Assessing Enclosure Modifications to Enhance Accessibility for Zoo-Housed Meerkats (Suricata suricatta)
papers.abstract: Scientific advancements have contributed to increased longevity of animals in zoos and aquariums, creating a growing need for environments that remain accessible to geriatric animals and animals with disabilities. However, few empirical studies have evaluated whether accessibility-focused enclosure modifications impact species-appropriate behavior. We evaluated the effects of accessibility modifications on a group of four adult zoo-housed meerkats (Suricata suricatta), including one individual with a forelimb amputation and one geriatric individual. Low-level logs and steps were added to the enclosure to provide intermediate heights and facilitate access to elevated areas. Following the introduction of these enclosure modifications, sentry behavior increased, with all individuals engaging in this behavior compared with only one individual during baseline. The meerkats also increased their overall use of low-elevated areas following modification, although individual responses varied. Posture differed between study phases, with meerkats more frequently adopting tri/quadrupedal postures following modification. Together, these findings suggest that relatively simple accessibility-focused modifications can expand opportunities for geriatric animals and animals with disabilities to engage in species-appropriate behavior. More broadly, this case study highlights the importance of empirically evaluating accessibility interventions and incorporating universal design principles into animal spaces to accommodate individuals with diverse physical abilities and promote positive animal welfare.

papers.title: Mathematical model of phenotypic plasticity predicts interconversion is a drug target for neuroblastoma.
papers.abstract: Neuroblastoma is a paediatric cancer arising from the sympathetic nervous system as neural crest cells, made up of noradrenergic (NOR/ADRN/N), mesenchymal like (MES/S), and intermediate (I-type/I) cell types. These cells can interconvert between types, contributing to treatment resistance and relapse. We developed a mathematical model to investigate how interconversion patterns affect the efficacy of phenotype-specific inhibitors. We used three ordinary differential equations to describe the dynamics of the three populations, including logistic growth, interconversion, and drug-induced death. Of the 64 possible interconversion patterns, five reduced the target population: two for N cells and three for S cells. N targeting patterns were more effective with higher interconversion rates, while mesenchymal targeting patterns were more effective with lower interconversion rates. Stability analysis revealed that natural tumour growth was always unstable, but during treatment, N-suppressing patterns combined with an S inhibitor gave the most consistently stable origin. Testing multi-stage and cyclic treatment schedules revealed that N-suppressing patterns with an S inhibitor, followed by an S-suppressing pattern with an N inhibitor, achieved more reliable remission. Three of the five patterns of interest correspond to reported biological plausibility, and known compounds exist to induce most of the required transitions, supporting the clinical relevance of these strategies for improving neuroblastoma treatment outcomes.

papers.title: A hawkmoth's point of view - Innate symmetry preferences are informed by floral display and foraging function in an insect pollinator
papers.abstract: Floral visual cues are key for flower recognition and feeding in many pollinators. In insects, innate preferences for characteristic floral colour and pattern cues can guide naive foragers during their initial foraging. Symmetry is suggested to be one such foraging cue, since it is a remarkably conserved floral feature, with flowers mainly displaying radial or bilateral morphologies. Insect pollinators like honeybees, bumblebees, and hoverflies have been found to distinguish symmetry from asymmetry spontaneously or through learning. However, whether innate preferences for floral symmetry types, i.e. radial or bilateral, influence naive flower choice, and whether such preferences are linked to functional benefits during foraging remains uncertain.We investigated innate symmetry choice and its associated foraging function in the hummingbird hawkmoth (Macroglossum stellatarum). Besides relying on pattern cues for flower choice, these hawkmoths feed while hovering, making symmetry a valuable visual cue for flight and proboscis control. In choice assays, the hawkmoths' innate preferences for symmetry types depended on the floral display planes, with considerable differences between the horizontal and vertical displays. Tracking the hawkmoths during foraging revealed that in both display planes, the innately preferred patterns increased foraging success by guiding approach and nectary search. While an analysis of flowers visited by hawkmoths in nature did not reveal the same link between symmetry and display plane, a majority of plant species with vertically displayed flowers showed features matching those innately preferred by the hawkmoths. In this study, we provide the first instance of display-dependent innate foraging preferences and highlight how visuomotor strategies in nectivorous insects may have coevolved with flower features.

papers.title: Hazard Structure and Repair Kinetics: A 2x2 Classification that Resolves the Stochastic-Death / Individual-Tolerance Dilemma
papers.abstract: The two variants of GUTS (General Unified Threshold model of Survival), stochastic death and individual tolerance, disagree about no-effect concentrations under time-variable exposure, and no standard test separates them. Each variant fixes two independent choices, which form a 2x2 classification: whether the hazard accumulates while damage exceeds a threshold (cumulative) or is set by the highest damage reached (peak-based), and whether repair is proportional or saturating. Calibration fit cannot choose: each structure fits by adjusting its own damage recovery, the cumulative one faster in twelve of fourteen compounds. For two identical pulses separated by complete recovery, the cumulative hazard predicts equal survival through both whatever the parameters, so a carry-over ratio (second-to-first survival) above one excludes it; in Gammarus pulex fourteen of fifteen ratios are at or above one, seven significantly. The peak-based hazard predicts the maximum of the ratio, approached as intervals lengthen in five of six compounds. For organophosphates, whose recovery outlasts the published pulse intervals, the one test on measured damage favours the peak-based hazard: diazinon-exposed Daphnia magna stopped being immobilised once acetylcholinesterase, still inhibited, began to recover. The peak-based hazard is the appropriate default for toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic risk assessment of narcotics and uncouplers, and provisionally of organophosphates.

papers.title: The Test Used to Choose Between Pesticide Survival Models Tracks Lesion Persistence, Not Hazard Structure
papers.abstract: Aquatic pesticide risk assessment predicts survival with toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic models that offer two hazard structures, cumulative or peak-based, which disagree about which exposure patterns are dangerous; for imidacloprid, published choices differ across eight species. The choice is made from one observation: deaths after transfer to clean water are taken to refute the peak-based structure. That inference holds only if damage is falling, which is not measured in these tests but taken from a fitted model. The observation responds to the compound and design, not the hazard structure. Across thirty-two Gammarus pulex treatments the post-exposure death rate places anticholinesterases above uncouplers, in the order of lesion persistence. For diazinon, one series returns opposite verdicts over its sixteen-day window and its first four days. For imidacloprid in Daphnia magna, one damage stage favours the cumulative structure by 78 likelihood units and two stages the peak-based one by 7. Four conditions make a design informative; thirteen of thirty-six treatments in a thirteen-compound archive meet them. Spreading a fixed exposure over longer intervals raises mortality in one of five species, which no repair law reproduces with the kinetics of the models. For neonicotinoids, predictions for such patterns are unvalidated, not conservative.
